newsitem.title: FRANCE: New chink opens in French anti-privatisation stand.
newsitem.headline: New chink opens in French anti-privatisation stand.

text.p: France's Socialist-led government has pleased its supporters by scrapping the sale of giant defence supplier Thomson-CSF but it is nevertheless looking increasingly pragmatic on privatisation.

Diluting its campaign pledges, the six-week-old government has already questioned the value of costly public bail-outs in the troubled financial sector and promised to put national interest above ideology in weighing state sell-offs.

Stock markets pounced on that pledge by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on July 3 as evidence that his cabinet will not stand in the way of banking and insurance privatisations planned by its centre-right predecessors.

Expectations have also grown that the government, which put all privatisations on ice after its upset election victory on June 1, will let a minority stake in France Telecom be floated to help it prepare for Europe-wide competition in 1998.

Friday's statement announcing the cancellation of the Thomson-CSF selloff may have lowered the threshold further, since it said only that the state would keep a "decisive" stake in Europe's top defence electronics supplier.
That appeared to hint at a blocking minority alongside private partners or a "golden share" to protect the nation's security interests rather than majority control.
The state currently holds 58 percent of Thomson-CSF which employs 46,000 people worldwide, two-thirds of them in France.

Weekend press reports said Jospin's office, in charge of the negotiations, was considering allowing the state's share in Thomson-CSF to slip below 50 percent through an injection of new outside capital or the creation of a joint entity with partners.
But to keep his election pledges, Jospin had drawn the line at selling any of the state's stock in Thomson-CSF.

Facing a hole in the budget and pressure to cut deficits to qualify for European monetary union, the government needs money to fund campaign promises to reduce youth unemployment and the working week, as well as recapitalising other state firms.
While it cannot directly grab privatisation proceeds to cut the deficit, new cash would help it indirectly by financing those badly needed capital injections.

A partial sale would also allow firms such as Thomson-CSF and France Telecom to make key strategic alliances with European partners such as Britain's GEC and Germany's Daimler Benz Aerospace or Deutsche Telekom, which distrust France's traditional state direction of industry.
Jospin must however weigh this benefit against opposition to sell-offs from militant trade unions and the Communists who hold junior cabinet posts and the balance of power in parliament.

Le Journal du Dimanche newspaper said the government planned a compromise keeping "at least a blocking minority of 33 percent but not necessarily 51 percent" in Thomson-CSF. Others said the probable target stake for the public was 40 percent.

Engineering giant Alcatel Alsthom, which bid for Thomson-CSF against missile conglomerate Lagardere, was seen emerging as the government's outside partner, with a further residue of 20 percent being traded on the Paris bourse.
A government spokesman said no decisions had been taken.
French markets, which reopen on Tuesday after the Bastille Day holiday weekend, have been waiting for weeks for clarification of the new government's line on privatisations.
Brokers say investors are convinced a minority stake in France Telecom will be sold this year after staff consultation.
The previous government had planned to sell 30 to 35 percent in what would have been France's biggest stock market operation.
A recent poll showed most French voters support the sale of part of France Telecom.
Economists say an audit of France's stretched finances due on July 21 could give Jospin the political weapon he needs to press the button on a string of state auctions.

While the government has leaned against selling flag carrier Air France, or losing control of public services, it has shown least resistance to floating off financial firms nationalised by previous Socialist administrations in the 1980s. Most have since had to be rescued from heavy property losses or dud loans.
"I wouldn't be totally surprised if (state-owned) banks and insurance companies were put on the market pretty fast," a senior government source said, without elaborating.

Analysts believe the government will sell insurer GAN and regional banking arm CIC and eventually Credit Lyonnais, whose ill-fated expansion in the early 1990s cost the taxpayer an estimated 100 billion francs ($16.6 billion). ($ = 6.021 French Francs)
